parsed_answer.content:
In the Spring Framework, stereotyping classes is the primary mechanism for declaring beans via component scanning rather than explicit XML or Java configuration. A stereotype annotation is a specialized meta-annotation that decorates a class to indicate that it plays a specific role in the application architecture, fulfilling the contract of the Dependency Injection container. While functionally identical at runtime—as they all ultimately register a BeanDefinition with the BeanFactory—they carry immense semantic and architectural value.

The root of all stereotypes is `@Component`, a generic marker for any Spring-managed component. However, as enterprise architectures grew, the Spring team introduced specialized semantic variants: `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller`. Each of these annotations is meta-annotated with `@Component`, meaning Spring's classpath scanner treats them with the exact same bean-creation lifecycle. The true differentiator lies in how infrastructure components, persistence exception translators, and aspect-oriented programming (AOP) pointcuts target them.

The `@Service` annotation denotes a business-layer component. While it currently does not add specialized behavior beyond `@Component`, it signals intent to human maintainers and leaves the door open for future framework optimizations, such as declarative transaction management pointcuts. The `@Repository` annotation serves the persistence layer and triggers Spring's powerful PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor. This translation mechanism automatically catches vendor-specific database exceptions (like SQLException from JDBC or Hibernate exceptions) and translates them into a unified, unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy, decoupling your business logic from underlying persistence technologies. Finally, the `@Controller` annotation identifies a web controller in Spring MVC. Beyond bean registration, it informs the DispatcherServlet that the class is eligible for handling incoming HTTP requests, often working in tandem with request-mapping handlers and view resolvers.

rows: Utility classes or generic beans that don't fit specific layers
Service-layer business logic and transactional boundaries
Data access objects (DAOs), repositories interacting with databases
Handling HTTP requests, returning views or REST responses

items: Classpath Scanning: Spring's ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner discovers stereotype annotations by inspecting class bytecode during startup using the ASM library, avoiding the performance overhead of loading every class via standard reflection.

Meta-Annotation Inheritance: Because @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are meta-annotated with @Component, you can write custom annotations that combine multiple traits (e.g., combining @Service and @Transactional into a single composite annotation).

Persistence Exception Translation: The @Repository annotation forces Spring to create a bean post-processor proxy around the class, intercepting native database exceptions and rethrowing them as runtime DataAccessExceptions to maintain architecture purity.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap is swapping out @Repository for @Component on a data access bean thinking 'they do the same thing.' Doing this breaks exception translation; your service layer will suddenly start catching raw, vendor-locked SQLExceptions or Hibernate exceptions instead of Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy, tightly coupling your business logic to your database vendor.

title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller? What is a stereotype annotation?
